title: C strings, character arrays and the null terminator
learningObjectives: Explain the null-terminated byte-string convention used by C library functions.
Distinguish a valid C string from an arbitrary character array.
Reserve storage for the terminating null character.
Use strlen and puts with valid null-terminated strings.
Recognize that string length in bytes may differ from the number of user-perceived characters.

understand.concept: C does not have a separate built-in string type. The standard library conventionally represents a string as a sequence of char elements ending with a null character, `\0`. A character array is not automatically a valid string: a null terminator must occur within the accessible array. Functions such as strlen and puts rely on that terminator to determine where the string ends.
understand.whyItMatters: This concept supports correct handling of C data and helps prevent invalid memory access or incorrect program behaviour.
understand.analogy: Think of the construct as a precisely bounded sequence of storage and operations.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's rules for object lifetime, bounds, types or undefined behaviour.

explain.narrative:
## 1. What is a C string?

A C string is a sequence of char values followed by a null character. The null character has value zero and is written as `\0` in source code. It is not the same as the digit character `'0'`.

## 2. Character array versus string

`char name[8]` is an array of eight characters, but it is not necessarily a valid string until a null character is stored within those eight elements. If the array contains no terminator, functions that expect a string may read beyond the object.

## 3. Reserve terminator space

To store up to seven non-null characters as a string, an eight-element array is required so the final element can hold `\0`. A string literal used to initialize an array includes its terminating null character in the required storage.

## 4. Standard functions

`strlen` counts the bytes before the first null character and does not include the terminator. `puts` writes a string and appends a newline. Both require a valid null-terminated string.

## 5. Text encoding

A byte-oriented C string may contain a multibyte encoding such as UTF-8. strlen reports bytes before the terminator, not necessarily visible characters or grapheme clusters. Unicode-aware text processing needs additional encoding-aware logic.

examples.title: A character array initialized from a string literal
examples.explanation: The array includes storage for the null terminator. strlen counts the characters' encoded bytes before that terminator.

examples.title: Reserve room for the null character
examples.explanation: The fourth element explicitly terminates the string. Without it, puts would not know where the string ends.

questions.prompt: What marks the end of a conventional C string?
options: The array's last allocated byte automatically
questions.explanation: C string functions scan until the null character.

questions.prompt: How many array elements are needed to store up to 7 visible single-byte characters as a C string?
questions.explanation: The storage must include one additional element for the null terminator.

options: Bytes before the first null character
The number of Unicode grapheme clusters
questions.answer: Bytes before the first null character
questions.explanation: strlen returns the number of char elements before the terminator.

questions.prompt: Is every char array automatically a valid string?
options: No; it must contain a null terminator within its accessible storage
Yes, every array is automatically terminated
Only arrays with an even length
questions.answer: No; it must contain a null terminator within its accessible storage
questions.explanation: A character array may contain arbitrary bytes and no terminator.

questions.prompt: Can strlen always be used to count user-perceived Unicode characters?
options: No; multibyte encodings mean byte count can differ from character count
questions.answer: No; multibyte encodings mean byte count can differ from character count
questions.explanation: strlen is byte-oriented and stops at the first null byte.
